pass_a_gloss: He will say in the ecclesiastical proclamation that the word about the righteous anointing of God is contained, which, being believed to be true, also provokes to living well and fleeing from sin in every way, so that we may understand, having been reconciled to God, the most necessary problem. And so that we may understand what free will is, it is necessary to unfold the concept of it, so that with it having been clarified, what is being sought may be presented clearly. For of the things being moved, some have the cause of movement in themselves, but others are moved only from outside. Therefore, the things being carried are moved only from outside, such as wood and stones and all matter that is held together by habit alone. But let the movement of bodies be set aside from the discussion now, since there is no need for this for the present topic. And animals and plants and, in short, all things that are held together by nature or soul have the cause of movement in themselves: from which they say metals are, and also fire is self-moving, and perhaps also springs. And of the things having the cause of movement in themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, but others from outside themselves: from outside themselves, indeed, the inanimate things, but from themselves, the animate things. And the animate things are moved from themselves, a fantasy occurring, which provokes an impulse. And again, in some of the animals, fantasies occur, provoking an impulse, with their nature, which is imaginative, moving the impulse in an orderly way, as in the spider, a fantasy of weaving occurs, and an impulse follows to weave, with its imaginative nature provoking it in an orderly way to this very thing, and no other thing is believed by the animal after its imaginative nature. And in the bee, to shape wax. But the rational animal also has reason in relation to its imaginative nature, which approves the fantasies and rejects some, but accepts others, so that the animal may be led according to them. From which, since in the nature of reason there are starting points for contemplating the good and the bad, by following which, having contemplated the good and the bad, we choose the good, but turn away from the bad, we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy according to the opposite. But it must not be ignored that the greater part of nature, which is ordered to all things, is in the animals, and for the most part, or for the lesser part, so that it is near, I say, the work of reason in the tracking dogs and in the war horses. For the thing that comes to us from outside, moving a fantasy in us, such and such, is, to be sure, not in our power: but to judge whether to use what has happened in this way or otherwise, is the work of our reason, either working in us according to the starting points that provoke us to the good and to duty, or turning us away to the opposite.

pass_b_english: In the church's proclamation, the message about God's righteous anointing is contained; once it is believed to be true, it also provokes people to live well and to flee from sin in every way, so that we, having been reconciled to God, may grasp the most necessary problem. To grasp what free will is, we must unfold its concept so that, once clarified, the question at hand may be set out clearly. Some things that are moved have the cause of their movement within themselves, while others are moved only from outside. Things that are carried — wood, stones, and all matter held together by habit alone — are moved only from outside. Let us set aside from the discussion the motion of bodies as such, since it is not needed for our present topic. Animals, plants, and in short all things held together by nature or soul have the cause of movement within themselves; they say that metals belong among these, and that fire is self-moving, and perhaps springs as well. Among the things that have the cause of movement within themselves, some are said to be moved from themselves, others from outside themselves: the inanimate things are moved from outside themselves, the animate things from themselves. Animate things are moved from themselves when a fantasy occurs that provokes an impulse. Again, in some animals, fantasies arise that provoke an impulse, with their imaginative nature moving the impulse in an orderly way — as in the spider, where a fantasy of weaving occurs and an impulse follows to weave, because its imaginative nature provokes it to this very thing in an orderly way, and the animal believes nothing else after that nature; and in the bee, toward the shaping of wax. But the rational animal also possesses reason alongside its imaginative nature — reason that judges the fantasies, rejecting some and accepting others, so that the animal may be led according to them. Since the nature of reason contains starting points for contemplating the good and the bad, and by following them we contemplate the good and the bad, choose the good, and turn away from the bad, we are praiseworthy when we give ourselves to the practice of the good, but blameworthy when we do the opposite. Still, we must not ignore that the greater part of the nature ordered to all things exists in animals, and for the most part, or for the lesser part, so that the work of reason in tracking dogs and war horses is, so to speak, close at hand. To undergo something from outside that stirs a fantasy in us, one way or another, is, to be sure, not within our power; but to judge whether to use what has happened in this way or otherwise is the work of the reason within us — whether it acts in us through the starting points that provoke us toward the good and toward duty, or turns us away toward the opposite.
